records.title: Engine Oil Leaks from Rear Cam Seal O-Ring and Valve Cover Gasket (I5)
records.description: The inline-five 80/90 commonly develops oil leaks at the back of the cylinder head. The rear cam seal is essentially an O-ring on the silver dust cap at the rear of the camshaft; it hardens and cracks with age and weeps oil. Combined with an aged valve cover gasket, oil seeps down the back and sides of the engine, where it can mimic a rear main seal or oil pan leak and make diagnosis confusing. These are age-related rubber seal failures typical of 30-year-old engines and are a frequent source of the oily film and burning smell owners report.
records.solution: Replace the rear cam seal/dust-cap O-ring together with the valve cover gasket; owners report a bone-dry engine afterward. Clean the area first to correctly locate the source, since valve-cover oil migrates and can be mistaken for lower-engine leaks. Use correct Audi/VW seals and torque the valve cover evenly.
symptoms: Oil film down back/side of engine
Apparent rear-main/oil-pan leak that is actually higher up

records.title: Hydraulic Brake Pressure Accumulator ("Bomb") Nitrogen Loss and Loss of Brake Assist
records.description: The Audi 90 quattro uses a central Pentosin hydraulic system that powers both the power steering and the brake servo. A nitrogen-charged pressure accumulator (universally nicknamed the "bomb") stores energy to provide brake boost if the pump or engine quits. The nitrogen gradually diffuses through the internal diaphragm, so almost all accumulators degrade after roughly seven years of service. As the charge bleeds down, the brake warning light stays lit for several seconds after start-up and, with the engine off, the pedal loses its power assist after fewer than about ten pumps. A weak or failed bomb makes the brake pedal hard and unboosted, sharply increasing stopping distances. The shared hydraulic pump and servo can also leak, and using ATF instead of Pentosin ruins the seals and sticks the accumulator check valves.
records.solution: Test the bomb by counting assisted pedal strokes with the engine off (loss of assist in under ~10 strokes indicates a depleted accumulator). Replace the pressure accumulator (P/N 893 612 061 C for pre-10/89 or 4A0 612 061 D for 1990-91), renewing the copper sealing washers/O-rings, and perform a complete Pentosin (CHF 11S) flush and refill with about 1 liter. If the fluid is old or dirty, a full bleed/refill may free a stuck valve before replacement is needed. Never substitute ATF. Inspect the hydraulic pump and servo return line for leaks at the same time.
symptoms: Brake warning light stays on several seconds after starting
Loss of brake boost after a few pedal pumps with engine off
Power steering and brakes feel heavy together

records.title: Hydraulic Valve Lifter Tick on Cold Start
records.description: The 2.8L V6 hydraulic valve lifters (hydraulic lash adjusters) bleed down overnight, causing a ticking noise on cold start that lasts 30 seconds to several minutes. Worsens with age and infrequent oil changes.
records.solution: Try switching to high-quality full synthetic 5W-40 oil with fresh filter. If tick persists beyond 30 seconds, replace hydraulic lifters. Using VW 502.00 spec oil is recommended. Short oil change intervals (5,000 miles) help prevent recurrence.

records.title: Speedometer / Odometer Plastic Gear Failure (B4 Triggers Check Engine Light)
records.description: The VDO instrument cluster in the 80/90 uses small plastic gears in the speedometer/odometer assembly that strip teeth or break with age, a well-documented failure across the B3 and B4 chassis. The speedometer needle and odometer typically quit together. Crucially, on B4 cars the speed signal also feeds the engine ECU, so when the gear fails the ECU loses its vehicle-speed-sensor (VSS) signal and illuminates the MIL/check-engine light along with the dead speedometer. The original pot-metal/plastic gears are the weak point.
records.solution: Replace the failed speedometer/odometer gears with an aftermarket repair kit; Delrin replacement gears outlast the originals. The trip-odometer reset linkage can also break, so handle it carefully. On B4 cars, confirm the dead speedometer is the cause of the MIL before chasing other VSS faults. Repair is typically a cluster-out bench job.
symptoms: Check engine light / MIL on B4 models
Whirring or clicking noise from cluster

records.title: Timing Belt Failure Causing Bent Valves (Interference Engines NG/7A I5 and AAH V6)
records.description: All Audi 90 engines of this era - the NG and 7A 2.3L inline-fives and the AAH 2.8L V6 - are interference designs. If the rubber timing belt snaps, stretches, or jumps teeth, the pistons strike the open valves and bend them, turning a routine service item into a major engine repair. The belt, tensioner, and water pump are wear items; the belt can crack or stretch with age and the tensioner pulley weakens over time, allowing incorrect cam timing, misfires, or sudden engine stoppage. Owners are repeatedly warned that the AAH 12-valve V6 in particular is an interference engine where a broken belt means bent valves. Because these cars are now 30+ years old, belts often fail from age rather than mileage.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt, tensioner(s), and water pump together as a set on the manufacturer interval (roughly every 60,000 miles) or every 5-7 years regardless of mileage. Inspect the old belt for cracks/glazing and verify cam-to-crank timing marks on reassembly. On the V6 confirm correct tensioner setup, as incorrect timing causes immediate stoppage. Document the last belt service when buying one of these cars; if unknown, treat replacement as immediate maintenance.
symptoms: No-start with low compression after belt break

records.title: Wandering / Erratic Idle from Idle Stabilizer Valve and Intake Vacuum Leaks (I5)
records.description: A very common complaint on the inline-five Audi 90 (NG and especially the 20-valve 7A) is an unstable idle that hunts between roughly 400 and 1600 RPM and sometimes stalls. The root causes are a dirty or electrically faulty Idle Stabilizer Valve (ISV) - the Hitachi unit on early 1990 cars sits on the airbox/side of the intake - and unmetered air entering through vacuum leaks. The most frequent leak points on the 7A are the rubber splitters on the back of the intake manifold, the fuel pressure regulator vacuum line, a decomposed O-ring at the idle screw, and cracks in the rubber boot between the air sensor/filter housing and throttle body. Cold-start erratic idle and stalling are typical first symptoms.
records.solution: Remove and clean the ISV with carburetor cleaner (soak/disassemble the Hitachi unit if needed) and verify its electrical connector and ground. Smoke-test or visually inspect intake vacuum lines, replacing cracked intake splitters, the FPR vacuum hose, the throttle-body boot, and the idle-screw O-ring. Reset base idle per spec after cleaning. Most cases resolve without parts beyond seals and the cleaned valve.
symptoms: Stalling at idle or when coming to a stop

records.title: Water Intrusion into Footwells from Windshield Base and Sunroof Drains Damaging Electronics
records.description: B4-generation Audi 90/80 cars are notorious for water leaking into the front floor pans. Owners report water entering around the lower corners of the windshield and pooling in both front footwells, with the same pattern seen on nearly every junkyard B4. A second path is the sunroof drain system: the drain channels are poorly designed where the tubes connect, and the channel holes on both sides clog, causing water to overflow into the cabin. Water-soaked carpet and headliner create condensation and can short-circuit sensitive electronics (including modules near the ECU cover, where trapped debris blocks drainage). Left unaddressed it leads to corrosion and electrical faults.
records.solution: Clear and flush the sunroof drain channels and tubes; verify they exit freely. Inspect and reseal the windshield base/lower corners (a recently fitted windscreen can also be the culprit) and the ECU cover area, removing leaf debris so water drains. Dry out and treat any soaked carpet/insulation to prevent corrosion and electrical shorts.
symptoms: Intermittent electrical faults from water-damaged modules

records.title: Power Window Regulator Cable Failure
records.description: The cable-driven power window regulators in the Audi 90 are prone to cable fraying and snapping, causing the window to drop into the door or become stuck. The driver side fails most frequently due to heavier use.
records.solution: Replace the window regulator assembly. Lubricate the window channels with silicone spray during installation to reduce stress on the new regulator cables.

records.title: Window Regulator Clip and Cable Failure
records.description: The plastic clips that attach the window glass to the regulator break, causing the window to drop into the door. The cable-driven regulator mechanism also frays over time. Very common failure on all four doors.
records.solution: Replace window regulator assembly. Aftermarket regulators with metal clips are more durable than OEM plastic clips. Lubricate window channels with silicone spray during installation.
